cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and every locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu<\infty\), \[\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)\le C\int_{\mathbb R^n}\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)?\] The same constant must work for all dimensions, measures and admissible functions. This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: All norms and derivatives are Euclidean, with \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2)^{1/2}\). Here a log-concave probability measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho(x)=e^{-V(x)}\) of integral one, where \(V:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is measurable and convex; \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Convexity means \(V((1-s)x+sy)\le(1-s)V(x)+sV(y)\) for all \(x,y\) and \(0<s<1\), using the extended-real convention on the right. Thus \(d\mu(x)=\rho(x)\,dx\). Isotropy means finite second moments and \(\int x_i\,d\mu=0\), \(\int x_i x_j\,d\mu=\delta_{ij}\) for every \(i,j\), where \(\delta_{ij}=1\) if \(i=j\) and zero otherwise. Equivalently, the mean vector is zero and the covariance matrix is the identity. Isotropy excludes measures supported on a proper affine subspace, so no lower-dimensional singular case is omitted by using a density. Locally Lipschitz means that every point has a neighborhood on which \(|f(y)-f(z)|\le L\|y-z\|_2\) for some finite \(L\); the neighborhood and constant may depend on the point. Such a function has a Euclidean derivative outside a Lebesgue-null set, and \(\nabla f\) is the vector of its partial derivatives there; set it to zero where the derivative does not exist. This choice on the null set does not affect integration against \(\mu\). Write \(\bar f=\int f\,d\mu\), which is finite by the second-moment assumption, and \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int(f-\bar f)^2\,d\mu\). The gradient energy is the integral of \(\|\nabla f\|_2^2\). Define \(C_{\mathrm P}(\mu)\) as the infimum of all \(a\ge0\) for which the displayed inequality holds with \(a\) for every admissible function, with infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). The question asks whether these constants are uniformly bounded; it does not ask for their optimal universal value. No symmetry, product structure, differentiability of \(V\), bounded support or positive lower bound on its curvature is assumed. Uniform laws on full-dimensional convex bodies are included after isotropic normalization; a convex body is a compact convex set with nonempty interior. The problem is an analytic existence statement, with no oracle, encoding or algorithmic-time requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal Poincaré inequality with some finite real \(C>0\), or a Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: for every real \(C>0\), there exist an integer \(n\ge1\), a measure \(\mu\) satisfying all stated log-concavity and isotropy conditions, and an admissible locally Lipschitz \(f\) of finite second moment and finite gradient energy such that \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)>C\int\|\nabla f\|_2^2\,d\mu\). The dimension, measure and function may depend on \(C\). A single violation for one proposed numerical constant does not refute existence of some larger universal constant. A dimension-dependent bound, or a theorem restricted to linear, radial or quadratic functions or a narrower class of measures, is insufficient unless the proof also establishes the entire stated target. No optimal value of \(C\) is required. An equivalent geometric statement can qualify only with a Lean-checked implication proving this proposition or its negation; cited but unproved conjectural dependencies do not complete acceptance.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in \(O((N+1)^{c})\) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
cards.definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into \(S^{3}\); the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of \(S^{3}\) starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has \(O(n \log (n+1))\) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most \(C(n+d)^{k}\)?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with \(R^{d}\), where \(d\ge 1\), and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph \(G(\mathrm{P})\) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: No polynomial upper bound or superpolynomial counterexample for the stated worst-case edge-diameter problem was found through 11 September 2026. Natura’s 2026 result resolves the circuit analogue and explicitly leaves the combinatorial problem open. The card includes bounded and pointed unbounded polyhedra, counts facets, and imposes neither monotonicity nor an efficient path-finding requirement.

cards.title: Planar k-set extremal function
cards.formal: Let \(K_{2}(n,k)\) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets \(S\subseteq \mathrm{P}\) of size k strictly separable from \(P\setminus S\) by a line. Determine \(K_{2}(n,k)\) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with \((a,b)\ne (0,0), ax\)+by<c for every \((x,y)\in S\), and ax+by>c for every \((x,y)\in\)\(P\setminus S\). The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression \(F(n,k)\) and absolute constants \(0<c_{0}\le C_{0}<\infty\) such that \(c_{0}F(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le C_{0}F(n,k)\) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values \(n/2<k<n; k=0,n\) each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine a positive function \(F(n,k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(cF(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le CF(n,k)\) throughout \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Prove the universal upper bound and existence of matching point sets for every parameter pair in Lean. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required; a mere restatement of the defining extremum is insufficient. This asymptotic-complexity target uses constant-factor precision, not additive 0.01. A fixed-k result or the halving case alone does not determine the whole function.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate \(\eta\) with \(0<\eta <1/2\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret \(s\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), recovers s with probability at least \(2/3\) from independent samples \((a,\langle a,s\rangle \oplus e)\), where a is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and e is independently \(Bernoulli(\eta )\)?
cards.definitions: The inner product \(\langle a,s\rangle\) is \(\sum_{i} a_{i} s_{i}\) modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with \(\Pr [e=1]=\eta\). The learner knows n and the fixed rate \(\eta\), and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed \(\eta\) the algorithm and its polynomial bound \(p\eta\) may depend on \(\eta\), but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most \(p\eta (n)\) bit operations and requests at most \(p\eta (n)\) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational \(\eta\) does not demand a running-time bound uniform as \(\eta\) approaches \(1/2\) with n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n, 2^{k}\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with uniform-distribution error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(0\le k\le n, a k\)-junta is a function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) for which there is an unknown set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}, |S|\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that \(f(x)=g\)(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer \(t\ge 3\), setting \(\varepsilon =1/t\). Each requested example consists of an independently uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) and its exact, noiseless label \(f(x)\). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least \(2/3\) over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that \(h(x)\ne f(x)\) is at most \(1/t\). One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most \((n+2^{k}+t)^{C}\) steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal:
Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and absolute positive integers \(a,d\) such that the following holds for every pair of integers \(n,s\ge1\), every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most \(s\) terms, every probability distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), and every pair of integers \(t,b\ge2\)? Given only \((n,s,t,b)\) and access to independent labeled examples \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim D\), the learner halts within
\[a(n+s+t+b+1)^d\]
steps on every run and outputs an explicitly encoded deterministic Boolean circuit \(h\) on \(n\) inputs such that
\[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}D(x)\,\mathbf 1[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge1-2^{-b}?\]
The outer probability includes the learner’s coins and sampled examples. Membership queries, equivalence queries and descriptions of \(f\) or \(D\) are not supplied. The output need not be a DNF; it must be an efficiently evaluable circuit as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation, \(1\le i\le n\). A term is the conjunction of a subset of literals with at most one sign for each variable; the empty conjunction equals \(1\). A disjunctive normal form (DNF) is the disjunction of finitely many terms; the disjunction with no terms equals \(0\). Contradictory terms may be removed and repeated literals or terms ignored without increasing size. The size bound \(s\) counts terms, each of arbitrary width at most \(n\). The learner receives an upper bound \(s\), not a representation or a promise that the minimum DNF has exactly \(s\) terms. Both negated and unnegated literals are allowed.

The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and unit-cost transitions. The integer parameters are in canonical binary notation with separators. The runtime is polynomial in their displayed values, not merely their encoding lengths. Apart from the example oracle, it has no oracle or advice and performs no quantum operations. Reading parameters, processing samples, generating random bits, storing data, arithmetic and writing the entire hypothesis all count toward the same worst-case time bound. Internal random bits are independent unbiased coins, independent of the example stream.

Each example-oracle request returns a fresh independent pair \((x,f(x))\) from the same fixed \(D\) and target \(f\). The learner can choose when to request or reuse an obtained example, but cannot choose or condition the next sampled point. Transferring its \(n+1\) bits costs \(n+1\) steps, and subsequent processing is also charged. One may equivalently supply an infinite independent example stream and charge for each read example. All answers are noiseless. The algorithm receives neither point probabilities nor a sampling program for \(D\). The distribution is an arbitrary assignment of nonnegative real masses summing to one on the finite Boolean cube; no product structure, uniformity, smoothness or efficient samplability is promised. Thus finite exact sampling is an idealized access model, and the cost of implementing a sampler for \(D\) is not part of the learning task.

A hypothesis is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with input wires \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), constants \(0,1\), binary AND/OR gates, unary NOT gates and one designated output wire. It is encoded by its full topologically ordered gate list, gate types and binary indices of preceding wires, with separators, followed by the output index. The output is always valid circuit syntax. The number of written bits is bounded by the learner’s runtime; evaluation on any new \(n\)-bit input uses ordinary deterministic circuit evaluation, with time polynomial in \(n\) and the written circuit length. It uses no example oracle, target oracle or new randomness. A circuit that only describes a procedure for generating a much larger circuit is not an explicit output in this convention. No abstention output is allowed at prediction time.

The inner sum is the prediction error on a fresh point drawn from \(D\). The outer probability is over the finite sample/coin experiment bounded by the clock. The guarantee is required separately for every fixed \(f,D,n,s,t,b\); the same program and constants must work for all of them. No worst-case correctness on every point is required. With \(\varepsilon=1/t\) and \(\delta=2^{-b}\), the requirement is the usual polynomial dependence on \(n,s,1/\varepsilon,\log(1/\delta)\). Other \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1\) are covered by rounding to reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence at least as strong as requested. These encodings retain the original PAC target without an input representation for arbitrary real numbers.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence proposition or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify one learner and universal polynomial bound, establish valid explicit circuit output and the all-run time bound, and prove the stated error/confidence inequality for every target, distribution and parameter choice. A negative proof must rule out every uniform learner and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It must cover arbitrary circuit hypotheses, not only proper learners that return DNFs or a restricted algorithm class. A conditional lower bound whose computational assumption is left unproved, an algorithm with membership queries, a guarantee only for a special distribution or constant number of terms, and a superpolynomial runtime do not establish either full answer.

cards.title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
cards.definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified learner-existence statement or its negation in the specified arithmetic and sampling model. A positive answer includes the learner, its hypothesis representation, the polynomial training and evaluation bounds, and its distribution-independent accuracy guarantee. A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme for one-bit messages, with negligible correctness error and security against every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversary, in the plain model specified below? This is an unrelativized existence implication. The construction and its security proof may inspect the program of the one-way function and need not be black-box.
cards.definitions:
The security parameter is \(\lambda\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\), supplied as the unary string \(1^{\lambda}\). All algorithms are uniform classical Turing machines on bits: one finite program works for every parameter, with no advice, oracle or quantum resource. A PPT algorithm uses independent fair random bits and halts within a fixed polynomial in its total input length on every input and every random tape. Each algorithm has its own polynomial bound. Reading, computing, random-bit generation, communication and output all have ordinary bit-machine costs. Bit-string tuples use the component encoding \(s\mapsto1^{|s|}0s\); finite lists prepend an encoded binary component count. Binary integers have no leading zeros except the representation of zero. Explicitly proved polynomial-time equivalent encodings are acceptable.

A function \(\nu:\mathbb N_{\geq1}\to[0,1]\) is negligible if \(\forall d\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\exists\lambda_0\;\forall\lambda\geq\lambda_0:\nu(\lambda)\leq\lambda^{-d}\). A one-way function is a total deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) such that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(I\),
\[\Pr[\,|Y|=\lambda\ \land\ f(Y)=f(X)\,]\]
is negligible, where \(X\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and \(Y=I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\). The probability also includes the independent coins of \(I\). Any preimage of length \(\lambda\) counts as success; failure or a different output length does not. Injectivity and preservation of length are not required.

A candidate encryption scheme is a triple \((\mathsf{Gen},\mathsf{Enc},\mathsf{Dec})\) of uniform polynomial-time algorithms. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\) returns two finite bit strings \((pk,sk)\), the public and secret keys. The randomized algorithm \(\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b)\), for \(b\in\{0,1\}\), returns a finite ciphertext bit string \(c\). The deterministic algorithm \(\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,c)\) returns \(0\), \(1\), or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Algorithms are total on well-formed inputs, including arbitrary key and ciphertext strings; malformed encodings return a fixed failure response in polynomial time. Their runtime bounds use the full input length, so all honestly generated keys and ciphertexts have length polynomial in \(\lambda\). Encryption uses fresh private coins on each invocation, independently of key generation.

Correctness requires, for each \(b\in\{0,1\}\), negligible
\[\Pr[\mathsf{Dec}(1^{\lambda},sk,\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,b))\ne b],\qquad (pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda}),\]
over key-generation and encryption coins; failure counts as an error. This is average correctness over honestly generated keys and coins, not a requirement that every key and every random tape decrypt correctly.

Security requires that for every uniform classical PPT algorithm \(E\) outputting a bit, its advantage
\[\left|\Pr[E(1^{\lambda},pk,c)=B]-\frac12\right|\]
be negligible, where \((pk,sk)\leftarrow\mathsf{Gen}(1^{\lambda})\), \(B\) is an independent uniform bit, and \(c\leftarrow\mathsf{Enc}(1^{\lambda},pk,B)\). All coins, including those of \(E\), are independent except for the displayed dependencies. The programs are public. The adversary may perform any polynomial amount of computation and generate encryptions of arbitrarily chosen bits using \(pk\) and its own fresh coins; it has no decryption oracle. This is the standard one-bit indistinguishability formulation of chosen-plaintext security for public-key encryption. Security holds for every such adversary, with its own negligible bound eventually at all sufficiently large parameters. There is no restriction to infinitely many parameters, to an average choice of the adversary, or to a particular fixed polynomial attack time.

There is no pre-existing shared secret, trusted setup, random oracle, auxiliary hardness assumption or quantum information. The quantifier order is: if some \(f\) satisfying the stated one-wayness condition exists, then some single scheme satisfying the format, cost, correctness and security requirements exists. Neither its algorithms nor its proof must use \(f\) through an oracle interface. A uniform compiler taking the code of \(f\) as input is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this existence implication or its logical negation. A positive answer must obtain the stated uniform classical encryption scheme from the existence of one-way functions alone and prove the full correctness and chosen-plaintext guarantees. A negative answer must prove that a one-way function exists while no scheme in the stated class meets both guarantees. An oracle separation, a lower bound on a restricted class of reductions, a break of one proposed scheme, or a construction requiring some additional unproved hardness assumption does not settle the target. One-bit messages are the specified target; polynomially many independently encrypted bits yield the standard extension to longer messages with polynomial security loss. A cited or unchecked proof claim does not satisfy Lean acceptance.

cards.title: One-way functions from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) imply the existence of a classical one-way function secure against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inversion? Precisely, under that premise alone, must there exist one total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*}\]
such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time inverter \(I\) and every real constant \(c>0\), there is an integer \(N\ge1\) for which every \(n\ge N\) satisfies
\[\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,r}\!\left[z\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \land\ f(z)=f(x),\quad z=I(1^n,f(x);r)\right]\le n^{-c}?\]
Here \(U_n\) is the uniform distribution on length-\(n\) binary strings, and \(r\) denotes the inverter’s independent fair random coins. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as successful inversion. The function must be fixed before the inverter and security exponent are chosen.
cards.definitions:
All computation is by ordinary multitape Turing machines with fixed finite programs and finite tape alphabets, unit-cost transitions and explicitly encoded inputs/outputs. There are no oracles, nonuniform advice strings, quantum operations or external uncounted computations. Polynomial time means a bound \(a(m+1)^d\) on every input of length \(m\), for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on the machine. Reading input, evaluating functions, generating random bits and writing outputs are included in the running time.

A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) lies in \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic polynomial-time machine decides membership on every input. It lies in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership is equivalent to existence of a binary certificate of polynomially bounded length accepted by one deterministic polynomial-time verifier. The verifier is total on all input/certificate pairs. The premise compares these uniform total decision classes, not circuit classes or average-case classes.

The function \(f\) is computed by one deterministic machine in polynomial time on every binary string, including the empty string; its output length is consequently polynomially bounded. No length-preserving or injectivity requirement is imposed. Its description is public and may be built into an inverter’s fixed program. Security is required at positive input lengths \(n\).

An inverter \(I\) receives the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,y)\), with the input length \(n\) in unary and \(y\) a binary string. It has one fixed program, obtains independent unbiased coin bits, and halts within one polynomial in \(n+|y|+1\) on every input and every coin sequence. It outputs a finite binary string or the failure symbol \(\bot\). Its polynomial may depend on \(I\) but not on \(n,y\). An output of the wrong length, \(\bot\), or a string whose image differs from \(y\) is a failure. The retained convention is same-length inversion: a preimage must have the sampled input length \(n\). The original sampled \(x\) need not be recovered if another such preimage exists.

The experiment first draws \(x\) uniformly from all \(2^n\) inputs, evaluates \(y=f(x)\), and runs \(I\) with fresh independent random coins. Thus outputs with more length-\(n\) preimages are encountered more frequently; \(y\) is not sampled uniformly from the range. The probability is a finite exact average, since the inverter has an all-path polynomial clock. The constants in the forward evaluation bound and the inverter bound can differ.

Negligible inversion probability means exactly the quantifier order
\[\exists f\ \forall I\ \forall c>0\ \exists N=N(f,I,c)\ \forall n\ge N.\]
Neither the inverter nor \(f\) can vary with the input length, although each may use the supplied length in its computation. Security at only infinitely many lengths is not the target. Failure of one-wayness for a fixed \(f\) means that some single polynomial-time inverter has success greater than \(n^{-c}\), for some fixed \(c>0\), at arbitrarily large lengths; the logical negation does not demand success at every sufficiently large length.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the implication in the statement or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must establish, under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, a total function with one uniform polynomial-time evaluator and the stated eventual negligible-success guarantee against every permitted inverter. No additional circuit lower bound, average-case hardness assumption or conjectured cryptographic primitive may be left unproved. The proof may use the premise without proving it separately.

A negative proof must establish \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) and show that for every total deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\), there exist a single permitted inverter \(I\) and a constant \(c>0\) such that for every threshold \(N\), some \(n\ge N\) has inversion success greater than \(n^{-c}\). An oracle separation, a barrier to one reduction technique, or an efficient inverter for a particular candidate is insufficient. The target is an existence implication and imposes no black-box-construction requirement or prescribed proof method.
cards.status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. cards.title: Circuit obfuscation from polynomial-hard LWE
cards.formal: Does the decisional LWE assumption with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation for all polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no additional hardness, leakage-resilience, or circular-security assumption? The target is a classical polynomial-time obfuscator secure against classical polynomial-size adversaries.
cards.definitions: Fix \(q(n)\) to be the least prime at least \(n^{4}\) for every integer \(n\ge 2\). Let \(\chi _{n}\) be the discrete Gaussian on Z with probability of e proportional to \(\exp (- \pi e^{2}/n^{2})\). The assumed LWE statement is: for every polynomial \(m(n)\), the ensembles (\(A,A s+e\) mod q) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable, where A is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m\times n}, s\) is uniform in \(Z_{q}^{n}\), the m coordinates of e are independent \(\chi _{n}\) samples, and u is independent uniform in \(Z_{q}^{m}\). Indistinguishable means every polynomial-size classical circuit family has negligible advantage in n; negligible means smaller than \(n^{- c}\) eventually for every constant \(c>0\). No secret-dependent leakage is supplied. An obfuscator O is a uniform probabilistic algorithm running in time polynomial in \(\lambda +|C|\) that outputs a Boolean circuit \(O(1^{\lambda},C)\) of polynomial size. Circuits are finite acyclic \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) circuits with fan-in at most two, a specified list of input and output bits, and explicit binary descriptions; |C| is description length. For every polynomial p, there is negligible \(\mu _{p}\) such that for every |\(C|\le p(\lambda )\), with probability at least \(1- \mu _{p}(\lambda )\) over the obfuscator’s coins the output circuit agrees with C on ALL inputs. For every pair of circuit sequences \(C_{0},\lambda\) and \(C_{1},\lambda\) with polynomially bounded, equal description lengths, the same input/output lengths and identical functions, their obfuscations are computationally indistinguishable against all polynomial-size circuit families. Both functionality and security quantify over all such circuits, without requiring an efficiently checkable proof of equivalence. There is no oracle, trusted setup, quantum state, or restriction to a special circuit family. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No construction from the plain polynomial-hard decisional-LWE assumption fixed here was identified. Existing multi-assumption and circular-security constructions do not settle it. Polynomial hardness, polynomial modulus/noise ratio, classical adversaries, arbitrary circuits and no auxiliary leakage are explicit choices that make the broad LWE-alone question unambiguous.

cards.title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
cards.definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer \(c\ge 3\) and polynomial sample count \(M(d)\), let \(q(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^{c}\), let s be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{d}\), let A be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{M(d)\times d}\), and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp (- \pi z^{2}/(4d))\), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and \((A,u)\), for independent uniform \(u\in Z_{q}^{M(d)}\), are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{Z,2\sqrt{d}}\); only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\to\)(pk,evk,sk), \(Enc(pk,b)\), Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by \(\mathrm{P}(\lambda )\), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in \(\lambda\) and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most \(p(\lambda )\) and all input bits \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t}\), decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals \(C(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t})\), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than \(\lambda ^{-a}\) eventually for every \(a>0\). No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.

cards.title: Sub-square-root share-size exponents in perfect secret sharing
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every monotone access structure \(\Gamma\) on \([n]\) with \(\varnothing \notin \Gamma\) and \([n]\in \Gamma\), there exists a perfect secret-sharing scheme for a uniform one-bit secret with \(\max _{i} \log _{2}|S_{i}|\le K\cdot 2^{cn}\), where \(S_{i}\) is the finite alphabet of participant i’s share?
cards.definitions: \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). An access structure \(\Gamma \subseteq 2^{[n]}\) is monotone when \(A\in \Gamma\) and \(A\subseteq B\subseteq [n]\) imply \(B\in \Gamma\). A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on \(\{0,1\}\) and shares \(X_{i}\in S_{i}\), where each \(S_{i}\) is a finite nonempty set. For each \(A\in \Gamma\) there is a deterministic map \(r_{A}:\prod _{i\in A}S_{i}\to \{0,1\}\) such that \(r_{A}((X_{i})_{i\in A})=B\) with probability one. For each \(A\notin \Gamma\), the conditional distributions of \((X_{i})_{i\in A}\) given \(B=0\) and \(B=1\) are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding \(\log _{2}|S_{i}|\) up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some universal \(K>0\) and \(0<c<1/2\) satisfy the stated worst-share bound for every permitted access structure, or prove the logical negation in Lean. A negative answer must show that for every such \(K,c\) some access structure admits no perfect scheme with that bound, allowing all finite share alphabets and all joint distributions in the definition. The object quantified over is a general scheme; it need not be linear or efficiently constructed.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. Nir’s August 2026 ECCC report, Theorem 1.5, claims a general scheme with maximal share size \(2^{0.496n+o(n)}\), directly implying the stated strict threshold after adjustment of the universal constant. The target and theorem were compared; the proof was not independently verified. This remains an uncertain claimed resolution.

cards.title: Quantum PCP conjecture with classical reductions
cards.formal:
Do there exist fixed positive integers \(k,d\) and a rational constant \(0<\varepsilon<1\) for which the following promise problem \(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon}\) is QMA-hard under deterministic classical polynomial-time many-one reductions? An instance specifies \(n\geq1\) qubits, \(1\leq m\leq(n+1)^d\) local terms \(H_1,\ldots,H_m\), and rational thresholds \(0\leq a<b\leq1\) with \(b-a\geq\varepsilon\). Each term acts on at most \(k\) qubits, has rational real and imaginary matrix entries, and satisfies \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\). For the normalized Hamiltonian
\[H=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m H_i,\]
distinguish \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\geq b\). The classical reduction requirement preserves the saved card’s variant; the cited survey’s standard formulation permits quantum reductions.
cards.definitions:
A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\), with basis \(|0\rangle=(1,0)\) and \(|1\rangle=(0,1)\). The \(n\)-qubit state space is \(\mathcal H_n=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes n}\). A pure state is a vector of norm one; a general state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator \(\rho\) of trace one on that space. The adjoint \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(M\) is Hermitian when \(M=M^*\). The order \(M\preceq N\) means that \(N-M\) is Hermitian and \(z^*(N-M)z\geq0\) for every complex vector \(z\). The symbol \(I\) denotes the identity on the relevant space.

A local term is specified by an increasing list of \(\ell\) distinct qubit indices, with \(0\leq\ell\leq\min(k,n)\), and the complete \(2^\ell\)-by-\(2^\ell\) matrix in lexicographic computational-basis order on these indices. It acts as that matrix on the listed tensor factors and as identity on all other factors. A zero-qubit matrix is a scalar multiple of the identity. The bounds \(0\preceq H_i\preceq I\) concern the embedded operator, equivalently its supplied local matrix. Different terms may overlap and need not commute. Repeated terms are allowed and counted in \(m\). No spatial geometry, bound on the number of terms touching one qubit, or common zero-energy state is required.

The ground energy is
\[\lambda_{\min}(H)=\min_{\|\psi\|=1}\langle\psi,H\psi\rangle
=\min_{\rho\succeq0,\,\operatorname{tr}\rho=1}\operatorname{tr}(H\rho).\]
Both minima range over all global states, including entangled ones; no circuit preparation or classical description bound is imposed on a state. The promise gap \(b-a\) separates the two input cases. It is not a gap between the first and second eigenvalues of one Hamiltonian. The normalization and the per-term bound fix the energy scale, so \(0\leq\lambda_{\min}(H)\leq1\).

The input is an explicit finite bit string. To fix an encoding, for a natural number \(u\) let \(w(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(w(0)=0\), and write \(E(u)=1^{|w(u)|}0w(u)\). Encode an integer by a sign bit followed by \(E\) of its absolute value: sign 0 is nonnegative and sign 1 is negative, with sign 0 for zero. Encode a rational by its integer numerator and its positive denominator in lowest terms. A complex entry is its real rational part followed by its imaginary rational part. The instance consists of \(1^n0\), then \(E(m)\), then the rationals \(a,b\), then the \(m\) terms. A term consists of \(E(\ell)\), its \(\ell\) indices encoded by \(E\), and its matrix entries in row-major order. There are no trailing bits. The entire length \(N\) counts every numerator, denominator, index and matrix entry. Matrix precision is part of \(N\), not a unit-cost real input. Strings failing these syntactic conditions or any stated matrix or threshold condition are outside the promise, as are valid instances with \(a<\lambda_{\min}(H)<b\).

Here QMA is the following class of promise pairs \(\Pi=(Y,N_0)\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). A verifier has one deterministic classical Turing machine that, given \(x\), outputs a quantum circuit \(V_x\) and its register sizes in time polynomial in \(|x|+1\). The circuit has polynomially many qubits and gates, with a designated witness register of \(w(|x|)\) qubits and all other qubits initialized to \(|0\rangle\). The function \(w\) is polynomial-time computable and polynomially bounded. The generator and all resource bounds are fixed for \(\Pi\), valid on all inputs, and have no advice or oracle. The witness may be any density operator on its register and need not have an efficient description.

Circuits use the fixed gate set consisting of the Hadamard gate
\[W=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\]
the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), and controlled-NOT, which sends \(|u,v\rangle\) to \(|u,u\mathbin{\oplus}v\rangle\) for bits \(u,v\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates are specified by their names and qubit indices. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the computational basis; outcome 1 is acceptance. Probabilities are given by the Born rule applied to the witness and zero ancillas after the circuit. For every \(x\in Y\), some witness is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in N_0\), every witness is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). There is no acceptance requirement outside \(Y\cup N_0\).

QMA-hardness under the required reductions means that for every such pair \(\Pi\), there is one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(R_\Pi\) that halts on every input \(x\) within \(C(|x|+1)^r\) bit steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,r\), outputs a classical binary string, and satisfies
\[x\in Y\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm yes},\qquad
x\in N_0\Rightarrow R_\Pi(x)\in(\mathrm{LH}_{k,d,\varepsilon})_{\rm no}.\]
Output writing is included in the time bound. On promised source inputs the output must obey every target condition, including the common locality and term-count bounds. Off the source promise no output guarantee is required, but the runtime bound still holds. The reduction may depend on \(\Pi\); \(k,d,\varepsilon\) must be chosen once before quantifying over \(\Pi\). Thus the order is \(\exists k,d,\varepsilon\;\forall\Pi\in\mathrm{QMA}\;\exists R_\Pi\). No random or quantum computation is allowed in \(R_\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full stated existence of constants and classical QMA-hardness, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must prove the reduction guarantees and their uniform polynomial resource bounds for all QMA promise pairs with one fixed target triple \((k,d,\varepsilon)\). A negative answer must establish that for every allowed triple there is a QMA promise pair admitting no qualifying classical reduction to that target problem. The source pair may depend on the triple. A lower bound on one proposed reduction, a counterexample only to a particular construction, an oracle separation, or an algorithm for a restricted Hamiltonian family is not this negation. A proof allowing only quantum reductions does not by itself prove the saved classical-reduction variant; conversely, refuting the latter need not refute the weaker standard formulation. Constant-gap hardness with growing locality, a theorem solely about preparation depth of low-energy states, or an interactive verification theorem does not meet this answer criterion.
cards.status_note: The general quantum PCP problem is explicitly open in Bafna–Vyas ECCC TR26-150 of 19 August 2026 and in the July 23 Simons talk abstract. This card retains its stronger saved requirement of deterministic classical reductions and labels that choice; the original survey uses quantum reductions. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full proof or refutation of the saved variant. NLTS, structural reduction results, interactive proofs and the reported combinatorial-gap result have different conclusions. Full cited proofs were not independently verified.

notes: Preserved the saved deterministic classical many-one reduction target, but qualified the title and recorded that it is stronger than the cited survey’s formulation permitting quantum reductions. No unproved equivalence between the two is asserted.

Specified QMA via a fixed finite universal gate set, arbitrary density-operator witnesses, a total uniform classical circuit generator, Born probabilities and fixed completeness/soundness. Made reduction quantifier order, bit costs and off-promise behavior explicit.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist one total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{such that}\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BPP}?\]
Both classes require a correct membership bit with probability at least \(2/3\) separately on every input. The quantum and classical models are uniform and have fixed polynomial resource bounds as defined below. The established containment \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) makes equality the other possible answer.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings, with membership bit \(\mathbf1_L(x)\); put \(n=|x|\), including \(n=0\). There are no excluded inputs or external promise.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that one finite classical probabilistic multitape Turing-machine program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) satisfy the following for every input \(x\): every coin sequence makes \(R(x)\) halt within \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\) steps with a bit output, and
\[\Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.\]
Each transition costs one bit step and can read at most one fresh independent fair bit. Equivalently, feed a uniform \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\) and ignore unused bits; the probability condition is exactly
\[3\bigl|\{z:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ge 2\cdot2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over all coin sequences, not expected time. The same program and constants work for all input lengths and all inputs of a length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Both models are ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

The target compares existence of a decider for each total language. It does not require a compiler transforming quantum circuit generators into classical programs, preservation of a particular polynomial exponent, sampling an entire quantum output distribution, or computing amplitudes. Correctness on an average input distribution is insufficient.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{BQP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BPP},\]
or its logical negation, equivalently \(\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) and hence \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm{BQP}\).

For strict containment, establish the uniform circuit family, its polynomial generation/size/register bounds and pointwise bounded-error correctness for one fixed language, then exclude every classical probabilistic program with any fixed polynomial worst-case bound and the stated correctness guarantee. A lower bound only against deterministic algorithms does not exclude BPP. For equality, prove that every total language satisfying the quantum definition has a classical decider satisfying the full BPP definition; reproducing its circuit amplitudes or output distribution is not required.

Conditional hardness, an oracle or query separation, a promise or sampling separation, and a lower bound against shallow or otherwise restricted classical circuits do not establish strict containment of these total-language classes. A faster quantum algorithm for a task without a matching classical lower bound is also insufficient. The error thresholds specify exact probabilities, not numerical acceptance tolerances.
cards.status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states strict total-language containment as Conjecture 11.5. Primary oracle separations, the August 2026 shallow sampling publication and the September 2026 language/promise oracle example retain their specified model or output restrictions. Bounded searches located no full matching unrelativized separation or equality claim. An unverified claim that P differs from both BPP and BQP does not decide this comparison. This review checks statement and source scope; it does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all subsequent literature.

cards.title: Area law for gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
cards.formal: For every fixed local dimension \(q\ge 2\), interaction range \(r\ge 1\), interaction incidence bound \(g\ge 1\), norm bound \(J>0\), and spectral gap \(\Delta >0\), is there a finite constant \(C=C(q,r,g,J,\Delta )\) such that every Hamiltonian H described below, on every square lattice \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), has unique ground state \(\psi\) satisfying \(S(\rho _{A})\le C|\partial A|\) for every \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(\mathrm{L}\ge 1\) be an integer, \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}=\{1,\ldots ,\mathrm{L}\}^{2}\) with open boundaries, and the Hilbert space be the tensor product of \(C^{q}\) over its sites. Write \(H=\sum_{a} h_{a}\), where each \(h_{a}\) is Hermitian and acts only on a nonempty support \(X_{a}\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) of diameter at most r in the maximum-coordinate metric. Each site belongs to at most g supports, counting terms with the same support separately, and the operator norm of every \(h_{a}\) is at most J. Suppose H has a unique normalized lowest-energy eigenvector \(\psi\) and its next eigenvalue is at least \(\Delta\) above the lowest eigenvalue. This is a gap of the entire Hamiltonian; no spectral-gap condition is imposed on subregions or subsets of terms. For \(A\subseteq \Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\), let \(A^{c}\) be its complement in \(\Lambda _{\mathrm{L}}\) and \(\rho _{A}=Tr_{A^{c}}(|\psi \rangle \langle \psi |)\) and \(S(\rho _{A})=- Tr(\rho _{A} \log _{2} \rho _{A})\), with \(0 \log _{2} 0=0\). The boundary \(\partial A\) is the set of nearest-neighbor lattice edges with exactly one endpoint in A; its cardinality is the boundary length in lattice units. Empty and full regions have entropy zero. The local parameters and C must be independent of L, A, and the actual interaction matrices. Interactions may vary from site to site and with L. They need not commute or share a simultaneous minimum-energy state; translation invariance and frustration freeness are not assumed. No approximation or state-preparation algorithm is requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The February and April 2026 results retain extra hypotheses; the general globally gapped 2D entropy area law remains unresolved. The formulation explicitly requires a size-independent constant and fixes the geometric boundary, interaction norms, local dimension, uniqueness, and global gap.

cards.title: Information-theoretic classical verification of quantum computation
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform interactive protocol \((\mathrm{P},V)\) for the following promise problem? Input is an explicit quantum circuit C over {H,T,CNOT}, starting on all-zero qubits, with one designated output bit and binary description length N. Let \(p(C)\) be the probability of output 1. YES instances have \(p(C)\ge 2/3\) and NO instances have \(p(C)\le 1/3\). V is a classical probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm and the honest P is a quantum polynomial-time algorithm; they exchange only classical messages. On every YES instance, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P]\(\ge 2/3\). On every NO instance, for every computationally unbounded cheating prover P*, Pr[V accepts after interacting with P*]\(\le 1/3\). Both honest running times, the number of rounds and total communication must be polynomial in N.
cards.definitions: H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT is controlled NOT. The circuit explicitly specifies its qubits and gates, with at most N qubits. The promise excludes intermediate acceptance probabilities; no answer is required there. The two parties know C. The verifier may use private classical random coins, but has no trusted quantum memory, operations or measurements. The honest prover starts without an input-dependent advice state and uses a uniform polynomial-size quantum computation with classical control. All communication is through a single classical interface to one prover. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary adaptive response strategies with no computational bound; probabilities include the verifier’s coins and any prover randomness or measurements. There is no trusted setup, shared secret, second noncommunicating prover or cryptographic assumption. Fixed constant completeness and soundness gaps are the target; no constant-round requirement is imposed. This circuit promise problem expresses verification for arbitrary BQP computations. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The April 2026 primary paper explicitly leaves this single-prover, information-theoretic question open. The May 2026 trusted-gate result changes verifier resources, and the February 2026 witness-preserving protocol retains LWE. Neither meets this card’s classical-verifier and unbounded-cheater requirements.

notes: Defined the finite-list meaning of explicit representation; it is not an extra construction requirement.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
cards.definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\). Is the following conjunction true for all total Turing-invariant functions \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\)? Part I: every such \(f\) is constant in Turing degree on a cone or computes its input on a cone. Part II: the relation \(\leq_M\) of Turing reducibility on a cone prewellorders the set \(\mathcal F\) of all such functions above the identity on a cone, and for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), its pointwise Turing jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)+1\) in that same prewellorder. All functions, cones, ordinals and quantifiers are interpreted within the stated set-theoretic universe.
cards.definitions:
Write \(\omega=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) and \(2^{\omega}=\{x:\omega\to\{0,1\}\}\). Such a real is identified with the subset \(\{n:x(n)=1\}\) of \(\omega\). Fix an acceptable effective enumeration \((\Phi_e)_{e\in\omega}\) of ordinary oracle Turing programs with natural-number inputs and outputs. The oracle answers membership queries in a real. Define \(x\leq_T y\) to mean that some index \(e\) satisfies \(\Phi_e^y(n)\downarrow=x(n)\) for every \(n\in\omega\), with no time bound. The single index computes the entire real, and may depend on \(x,y\). Define \(x\equiv_T y\) by mutual reducibility. A Turing degree is an equivalence class for \(\equiv_T\). The jump \(y'\) is the characteristic real of \(\{e:\Phi_e^y(e)\text{ halts}\}\). Any acceptable effective numbering gives the same induced operation on degrees.

A total function \(f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}\) is Turing-invariant when \(\forall x,y:\ x\equiv_T y\Rightarrow f(x)\equiv_T f(y)\). No computability, measurability, Borel definability, order preservation or uniform production of reduction indices is required. The quantifiers concern functions on reals with this invariance property; no choice of a representative from every Turing degree is assumed.

For \(a\in2^{\omega}\), the cone with base \(a\) is \(C_a=\{x\in2^{\omega}:a\leq_T x\}\). Being constant in degree on a cone means
\[\exists a,b\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\equiv_T b.\]
Being above the identity on a cone means
\[\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ x\leq_T f(x).\]
The base may depend on \(f\). Constancy is equality of degrees, not literal equality of output reals. A cone requirement holds for every real in that cone, not merely infinitely many reals or a set of full ordinary Lebesgue measure.

For invariant \(f,g\), define
\[f\leq_M g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists a\in2^{\omega}\;\forall x\in C_a:\ f(x)\leq_T g(x).\]
The base may depend on both functions; no single base must work for all comparisons. Set \(f\equiv_M g\) when both \(f\leq_M g\) and \(g\leq_M f\). Let \(\mathrm{id}(x)=x\) and \(\mathcal F=\{f:2^{\omega}\to2^{\omega}: f\text{ is Turing-invariant and }\mathrm{id}\leq_M f\}\). The prewellorder clause means that \(\leq_M\) is reflexive, transitive and total on \(\mathcal F\), and that the induced order on the set \(\mathcal F/{\equiv_M}\) is a well-order: every nonempty subset of that quotient has a least member. Its strict order is \([g]<[f]\) when \(g\leq_M f\) and \(f\not\leq_M g\). When this clause holds, \(\operatorname{rank}_M(f)\) is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly below \([f]\), with its least class having rank zero. The pointwise jump is \(f'(x)=(f(x))'\). The \(+1\) in Part II is ordinal successor, and the rank is computed in the full quotient above the identity, not a selected definable subclass.

The background \(\mathsf{ZF}\) is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. Full dependent choice \(\mathsf{DC}\) asserts that for every nonempty set \(S\), every relation \(R\subseteq S\times S\) with \(\forall s\in S\;\exists t\in S:\ sRt\), and every \(s_0\in S\), there is a sequence \((s_n)_{n\in\omega}\) starting at \(s_0\) with \(s_nRs_{n+1}\) for all \(n\). The axiom of determinacy \(\mathsf{AD}\) asserts that for every set \(W\subseteq\omega^{\omega}\), the following perfect-information game is determined. Players I and II alternate choosing natural numbers, with I moving at even-numbered stages starting at zero; I wins exactly when the resulting sequence belongs to \(W\). A strategy assigns a next move to every finite history at that player’s turn, and is winning if every infinite play compatible with it is won by that player. Determined means that one player has such a winning strategy. No regularity condition is imposed on \(W\). These are internal set-theoretic axioms; the full axiom of choice is not added to them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of both parts of the conjunction under \(\mathsf{ZF}+\mathsf{DC}+\mathsf{AD}\), or a refutation of at least one part under that same background. A refutation of Part I must establish the existence of an invariant function that is neither constant in degree on any cone nor above the identity on any cone. A refutation of Part II must establish failure of the stated full prewellorder or, when that prewellorder exists, failure of the exact jump-successor clause. A result only for uniformly invariant, Borel, regressive or order-preserving functions does not prove the full conjunction. Counterexamples obtained with the full axiom of choice do not refute the stated determinacy version. The Lean formalization must represent the set-theoretic background faithfully, for example through an internal set universe and its satisfaction relation, with all reals and functions interpreted there; importing ambient choice into that universe and deriving a contradiction with determinacy is not a proof of this target. No unproved classification or uniformity principle may be substituted for a required part.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
