cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
cards.definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal:
Does ordinary Frege polynomially simulate Extended Frege in proof size? For the two fixed systems and binary size convention below, determine whether
\[\exists C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \forall\varphi\ \forall\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\Rightarrow\exists\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\land |\rho|\le C(|\pi|+2)^{k}]\bigr).\]
Here \(\varphi\) ranges over all finite propositional formulas in the ordinary variables, and \(\pi,\rho\) range over finite binary strings. The constants are independent of the formula and of both proofs. This asks for existence of short Frege proofs of the same conclusions; it does not require a polynomial-time algorithm that finds them. Equivalently, for every tautology \(\varphi\), is its minimum Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm F}(\varphi)\) bounded by one fixed polynomial in its minimum Extended Frege proof size \(s_{\mathrm{EF}}(\varphi)\)?
cards.definitions:
Formulas are finite ordered syntax trees generated by ordinary variables \(x_i\), temporary extension variables \(e_i\), negation \(\neg A\), and material implication \(A\to B\), with \(i\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,\ldots\}\). Ordinary formulas contain no \(e_i\). A Boolean assignment gives each variable a value in \(\{0,1\}\); negation reverses this value and implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and consequent false. A tautology is an ordinary formula true under every assignment to its ordinary variables. Every syntactic occurrence is written separately: a formula is a tree, not a circuit with shared subformulas.

The fixed Frege calculus has precisely these three axiom schemes:
\[A\to(B\to A),\qquad (A\to(B\to C))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to C)),\qquad (\neg B\to\neg A)\to(A\to B).\]
Each occurrence of a scheme uses a consistent substitution of formulas for its metavariables \(A,B,C\). The only inference rule is modus ponens, deriving \(B\) from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\). A Frege proof is a nonempty finite sequence of ordinary formulas, each justified by an axiom instance or modus ponens, with the last formula its conclusion. There are no hypotheses, extension axioms or separate rules that substitute into an already derived line. Any earlier line may be reused arbitrarily often. Auxiliary ordinary variables not occurring in the conclusion are permitted.

Extended Frege uses the same schemes and modus ponens, and additionally permits a consecutive pair of extension lines \(e_i\to\theta\) and \(\theta\to e_i\). At this introduction, \(e_i\) has not occurred in any earlier line and does not occur in \(\theta\) or in the final conclusion. The formula \(\theta\) may contain any ordinary variables and extension variables from completed earlier pairs, but no other extension variables. Both lines are written explicitly. After the pair, \(e_i\) may occur in later axiom instances, modus-ponens lines and definitions. Every extension variable in any line must be introduced this way; the final conclusion contains none. Definitions are thus acyclic, and cannot assert arbitrary assumptions about the ordinary variables. There is no bound on formula depth, proof depth, number of extensions, or reuse of earlier lines. No tree-like restriction is imposed on the proof sequence.

Use the following fixed prefix-free binary encoding. For an integer \(t\ge0\), let \(b(t)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(t)=1^{|b(t)|}0b(t)\), where concatenation is intended. A formula uses tag 00 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(x_i\), tag 01 followed by \(E(i)\) for \(e_i\), tag 10 followed by the child encoding for negation, and tag 11 followed by the antecedent and consequent encodings for implication. A proof of \(m\ge1\) lines starts with \(E(m)\). Each line then consists of a three-bit justification tag and its entire formula encoding. Tags 000, 001 and 010 specify the first, second and third axiom schemes, respectively; the written formula must be an instance of the specified scheme. Tag 011 specifies modus ponens and is followed, after the formula, by \(E(a)E(b)\): for line number \(j\), the indices satisfy \(1\le a,b<j\), line \(a\) is \(A\), and line \(b\) is exactly \(A\to B\) where the current formula is \(B\). Tags 100 and 101 specify the first and second lines of an extension pair. They must occur consecutively with exactly the two formulas and freshness conditions above; no additional data are implicit. The other tags and all malformed encodings are invalid. Frege permits only the first four tags and no extension variables. The size \(|\pi|\) is the bit length of this entire string, including every formula occurrence, variable index, line count and inference reference.

The predicates in the question mean validity under these syntactic rules with the specified final formula, not mere semantic validity of an unverified proof string. The displayed finite calculus is a standard complete classical Frege presentation; the explicit pair convention, auxiliary-variable convention and binary annotations fix ordinary polynomially equivalent presentations of the source systems. In particular, the bit cost is not merely the number of inference steps. The minimum sizes are defined for tautologies, all of which have finite Frege proofs. A size simulation alone is the target; the stronger notion of p-simulation additionally requires a polynomial-time proof translation.
cards.answer_criterion:
Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed proposition or its logical negation for the fixed systems and encoding. A positive answer must establish one pair of constants \(C,k\ge1\) that works for every valid Extended Frege proof and supplies the existence of a Frege proof of exactly the same ordinary conclusion with the required size. A negative answer must establish
\[\forall C,k\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge1}\ \exists\varphi,\pi\;\bigl(\operatorname{EFProof}(\pi,\varphi)\land\forall\rho\,[\operatorname{FProof}(\rho,\varphi)\Rightarrow |\rho|>C(|\pi|+2)^k]\bigr).\]
The formula and Extended Frege proof may depend on \(C,k\); no additional uniform construction of a separating family is imposed. All validity, size and quantifier claims must be justified in Lean. Conditional comparisons, a particular expensive expansion, restricted proof systems, a quasipolynomial simulation, or a polynomial-time proof-search lower bound alone do not meet this criterion. This is a binary asymptotic proof-size comparison, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its polynomial bound.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.status_note: The August 2026 equivalent-formulations paper explicitly states that the total deterministic log-rank conjecture remains unresolved, with the square-root-rank upper bound. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified resolution. The new lifting proof and its comparison of suppressed logarithmic factors were not independently verified; fixed polynomial lower bounds and partition reformulations do not settle the universal conjecture.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist one finite real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every positive integer \(n\) and every function \(f:\{-1,1\}^{n}\to\{-1,1\}\), \[H(f)\le C I(f),\] where \(H(f)\) is the Shannon entropy in bits of the squared Fourier spectrum and \(I(f)\) is total influence for uniformly distributed inputs? The same \(C\) must work for all dimensions and all Boolean functions.
cards.definitions: Let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and give each \(x\in\{-1,1\}^n\) probability \(2^{-n}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{i\in S}x_i\), with empty product one, and \[\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x),\qquad q_S=\widehat f(S)^2.\] These are real coefficients and \(\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}q_S=1\). Define \(\eta(0)=0\) and \(\eta(t)=t\log_2(1/t)\) for \(0<t\le1\), where \(\log_2 t=\ln t/\ln2\). Then \[H(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}\eta(q_S).\] The sum includes the empty set and is not conditioned on nonempty spectral subsets or divided by the variance. For each \(i\in[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus i}\) negate coordinate \(i\) and retain all other coordinates. Set \[I_i(f)=2^{-n}\bigl|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})\}\bigr|,\qquad I(f)=\sum_{i=1}^n I_i(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|q_S.\] Influence uses an actual bit flip, with no additional probability of leaving that coordinate unchanged. All scalar Boolean functions are allowed; no balance, monotonicity, circuit-size, degree or efficient-computability promise is imposed. Constant functions satisfy \(H(f)=I(f)=0\). The inequality is non-strict, so it includes them.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal inequality for some positive finite constant, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must use the specified uniform measure, full squared spectrum, base-two Shannon entropy and total bit-flip influence for every \(n\) and every scalar Boolean function. A negative proof must establish \[\forall C>0\ \exists n\ge1\ \exists f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\},\quad H(f)>C I(f).\] The dimension and function may depend on \(C\); equivalently, the entropy-to-influence ratios of nonconstant Boolean functions must be unbounded. Defeating one numerical constant or checking finitely many truth tables is insufficient. No optimal value of \(C\), algorithm for finding counterexamples or numerical approximation is required.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked classical primary literature, explicitly reiterated in both August 2026 quantum papers. Bounded searches and version checks through 15 September 2026 found no proof or refutation of the universal scalar Boolean Shannon-entropy inequality. The June separated classes impose extra hypotheses, the coordinate-entropy estimates retain an extra term, and the August counterexamples are operator-valued or use non-Boolean complex phases. Li–Han’s December 2025 weaker-bound preprint was withdrawn for prior appearance of its result. Complete new preprint proofs were not independently verified.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge3\) such that no q-SAT decider A has a bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F, for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The width q may depend on epsilon but is fixed independently of the input. Equivalently, is \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\)? This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. The sequence \(s_q\) is nondecreasing: a decider for width q+1 also decides the width-q restriction after checking its syntax. Since every \(s_q\le1\), its limit exists. The quantified statement says that no fixed positive saving from the exponent 1 works for all fixed widths. Its negation is that there exists one real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that for each integer \(q\ge3\) there are a q-SAT decider \(A_q\) and constants \(C_q,d_q\) with \(t_{A_q}(F)\le C_q2^{(1-\varepsilon)n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_q}\) for every q-CNF formula F. The algorithm and polynomial factor may depend on q and the selected epsilon. There is no added requirement of one algorithm receiving q as an input, nor of an effective procedure generating \(A_q\) from q. Each individual machine is uniform over its formula inputs. Infima need not be attained; the equivalence uses the available slack between a limit below 1 and 1.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed deterministic all-width proposition, equivalently a proof that \(\lim_{q\to\infty}s_q=1\) or that this limit is strictly below 1. A refutation must establish one positive exponential saving valid at every fixed width, with the algorithm and polynomial factors allowed to depend on that width. A positive answer must exclude such a shared saving. Improvement at finitely many widths, a randomized algorithm, or a lower bound only under another unproved hypothesis does not by itself meet this criterion. The target is a yes/no assertion about the limit, not its numerical approximation.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized algorithm \(A\), a fixed rational constant \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), and a fixed constant \(C>0\) such that, on every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with arbitrary real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, \(A\) outputs the entire exact shortest-distance matrix with probability at least \(2/3\), while every run takes at most \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps? Here \(n\ge2\), and steps are measured in the comparison-addition real RAM with logarithmic-size index words defined below. The same program, exponent improvement and time constant must work for every graph size and every real weight assignment.
cards.definitions:
The vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input gives \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order. Each entry has a presence flag and, when present, one exact finite real weight. Thus there is at most one edge for each ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges have no weight and are represented by the flag, not by a large finite number. There is no bound on the magnitude, sign or precision of a real weight. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle of negative total weight, including negative self-loops.

A finite directed walk \((v_0,\ldots,v_k)\) has weight \(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}w(v_i,v_{i+1})\). The empty walk from a vertex to itself has weight zero. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\), the distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum weight of a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or the separate symbol \(+\infty\) if none exists. The no-negative-cycle promise ensures that every reachable minimum is finite and attained; nonnegative cycles can be removed, so a simple path suffices for distinct endpoints. In particular \(d_G(u,u)=0\). Zero-weight cycles and equal shortest distances are allowed. Output consists of all \(n^2\) exact distances in vertex-pair order, each a real value or an unreachable flag. Printing the vertices of every shortest path is not required.

The machine has one fixed finite program and two kinds of random-access memory cell: exact real cells and finite index-word cells. One real-cell load, store or copy, addition, subtraction, or comparison costs one step; comparison returns its trichotomy result as a word. These are the only operations inspecting real values. Real constants built into the finite program are restricted to \(0\) and \(1\); there are no arbitrary advice constants. A real value cannot be converted to its digits, an integer address, or its floor. Multiplication or division of real cells and operations packing several arbitrary reals into one word are not available.

For some fixed integer \(a\ge4\) chosen as part of the program's model, an index word has \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Word loads, stores, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) cost one step. Unsigned integer quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step; division by zero is an invalid computation. A shift of at least \(b(n)\) positions returns zero. Addresses are words. All accessed cells must fit in this address range; a new work cell starts at zero and each access is charged. Word operations can process indices, counters and comparison results; they do not reveal the representation of a real edge weight. The input matrix and initially empty work memory are the only input-dependent initial state.

The randomized instruction obtains one fresh independent fair bit per step. All preprocessing, table construction, memory access, random-bit generation, input reading and output writing are charged to the same runtime. There is no nonuniform table supplied for free, extra prediction, oracle, parallel work unit or quantum operation. The bound is worst case over the input and every coin sequence. For each fixed promised graph, the probability that the whole output matrix is correct must be at least \(2/3\); separate success probabilities for individual entries are insufficient. A deterministic algorithm is included by ignoring the coins.

The bound depends on \(n\), not the bit length or magnitude of weights, because the real operations are exact primitives. This is a classical real-operation question, not an ordinary bit-time algorithm for arbitrary real encodings. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to rational values in \((0,1]\) preserves existence of a fixed positive exponent saving; any positive saving implies a smaller such rational saving. No behavior is required on graphs violating the no-negative-cycle promise.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated algorithm-existence proposition or its full logical negation in this exact machine model. A positive proof must exhibit one finite uniform program and fixed constants, prove the promised-graph distance semantics and joint correctness probability, and charge every operation to the worst-case \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) bound. A negative proof must rule out every such program and every fixed positive exponent saving, including randomized programs.

A result for bounded integer weights, a restricted graph family, approximate distances, a single source, or additional accurate predictions does not settle this target. Neither does a lower bound restricted to one reduction method or to machines lacking the permitted word operations. An unproved APSP hardness hypothesis cannot serve as the proof of its own consequence here. A bound \(n^3/f(n)\) with only a subpolynomial saving \(f(n)=n^{o(1)}\) does not establish a fixed exponent saving; expected running time alone does not establish the specified worst-case bound. There is no additive or multiplicative error allowance in the distance output.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal:
Does \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Equivalently, is the following statement true?
\[\forall L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \Longrightarrow\ L\in\mathrm P.\]
Here \(\mathrm{BPP}\) requires one randomized polynomial-time machine whose probability of a correct answer is at least \(2/3\) separately on every input, including both members and nonmembers of \(L\). The proposed deterministic machine must decide the same total language correctly on every input in polynomial time.
cards.definitions:
A language \(L\) is a set of finite binary strings; its membership bit is \(\mathbf1_L(x)\in\{0,1\}\). Put \(n=|x|\), allowing \(n=0\). Computation uses finite multitape Turing-machine programs over fixed finite tape alphabets. Each ordinary tape transition costs one step. A randomized transition may read at most one fresh independent unbiased bit. There is no oracle, advice, quantum operation, input distribution or promise excluding some inputs.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there exist one randomized program \(R\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that, with \(p(n)=C(n+1)^d\), both of the following hold for every \(x\):
\[\begin{gathered}
 R(x)\text{ halts within }p(n)\text{ steps on every random tape and outputs a bit},\\
 \Pr[R(x)=\mathbf1_L(x)]\ge 2/3.
\end{gathered}\]
The probability is only over the internal fair bits. An exact finite interpretation is to supply a uniformly distributed string \(z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), ignoring its unused suffix. The probability condition is then the integer inequality
\[3\bigl|\{z\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}:R(x;z)=\mathbf1_L(x)\}\bigr|\ \ge\ 2\cdot 2^{p(n)}.\]
The time bound is worst case over both the input and every random tape, rather than an expectation. The error bound is pointwise: success on almost all inputs of a length does not suffice. The same constants apply at every length; an input-dependent exponent is not polynomial time in this definition.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm P\) means that there exist one deterministic program \(A\) and fixed positive integers \(C',d'\) such that for every binary string \(x\), the program halts within \(C'(|x|+1)^{d'}\) steps and outputs \(\mathbf1_L(x)\). Reading, writing, arithmetic and tape access all count toward time. The deterministic program and its constants may depend on the language and its randomized decider, but not on the particular input or its length.

The requested deterministic computation may use a different algorithm and a different polynomial exponent. The target does not require an effective compiler taking descriptions of randomized machines to deterministic ones. It asks for existence of a polynomial-time deterministic decider for each language in the class. Deterministic programs are also randomized programs that ignore their coins, so \(\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) holds directly. Sampling a distribution, returning a valid witness, and answering only promised inputs are different tasks from deciding this total membership bit.
cards.answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated inclusion, or of its logical negation
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \land\ L\notin\mathrm P.\]
A positive proof must establish existence, correctness and a uniform polynomial time bound for a deterministic decider of every language satisfying the randomized definition. A negative proof must give one fixed language with a single randomized decider meeting the full pointwise error and worst-case polynomial time guarantees, and prove that no deterministic program with any fixed polynomial time bound decides that language.

A result conditional on an unproved hardness assumption, a nonuniform circuit simulation, an oracle separation, a promise-problem separation, or a simulation valid only at some lengths does not settle the target. A lower bound for one simulation rule or one generator family does not exclude every deterministic decider. The probability threshold is exact; this is a yes/no question with no numerical approximation tolerance.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal:
Does there exist one deterministic finite-program algorithm \(A\) and absolute integers \(C,D\ge1\) with the following property? For every \(n,w\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\), all integers, the algorithm specifies an integer seed length \(s=s(n,w,p)\ge0\) and a function
\[G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{n}\]
with \(s\le Cq\), where \(q=\lceil\log _2 n\rceil+\lceil\log _2 w\rceil+p\), such that every length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program \(B\) satisfies
\[\left|\Pr_{u\sim U_s}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\sim U_n}[B(z)=1]\right|\le 2^{-p}?\]
Here \(U_k\) is the uniform distribution on the \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). Require \(A\) to compute both \(s(n,w,p)\) and any requested bit \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_i\), \(1\le i\le n\), in at most \(Dq\) work bits and \((nw2^p)^D\) steps per call, in the model below. The same algorithm, constants and generator family must work for every parameter triple and every permitted program.
cards.definitions:
A length-\(n\), width-at-most-\(w\) ordered binary read-once branching program consists of nonempty finite layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_n\), each of size at most \(w\), a start state in \(V_0\), an accepting subset of \(V_n\), and functions \(\delta_{i,b}:V_{i-1}\to V_i\) for \(1\le i\le n\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\). On input \(z\), the state is updated by \(\delta_{i,z_i}\) at step \(i\); \(B(z)=1\) exactly when the final state is accepting. The bit order is \(z_1,\ldots,z_n\). Transitions may merge states, including two equally labeled edges from distinct states; no regularity or permutation promise is imposed. The transition tables, start state and accepting subset are arbitrary finite, possibly nonuniform data. The generator receives none of them.

The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and a mode flag. In the seed-length mode its input is \((n,w,p)\) and its output is \(s(n,w,p)\) in binary. In the bit mode its input is \((n,w,p,u,i)\) and it outputs exactly one bit before halting. Integer parameters use canonical binary notation with separators; the seed is its full binary string, with leading zeroes retained. Inputs occupy read-only tapes whose heads are bounded by endmarkers. There is a fixed finite number of initially blank, semi-infinite work tapes over \(\{0,1,\square\}\), with heads moving by at most one cell per transition. Each distinct work-tape cell visited is charged two work bits, including blank cells. This fixed encoding of tape symbols only fixes a constant in the space bound. All counters, arithmetic, stored history and preprocessing are charged; output is write-only and cannot serve as storage. There is no advice, oracle, external clock or other uncounted memory. Each transition costs one time step. The required bounds hold on every valid call, for every seed and requested index. Only the requested bit must be output in bit mode; there is no requirement to store the whole length-\(n\) string.

Probabilities are exact uniform finite averages. In particular, a seed always has weight \(2^{-s}\), even if several seeds produce the same string; signed weights and externally assigned coefficients are not permitted. The parameter \(p\) controls additive error, not failure probability of a randomized construction: \(A\) itself is deterministic. With \(\varepsilon=2^{-p}\), the target is \(O(\log n+\log w+\log(1/\varepsilon))\) seed length and work space. Ceiling conventions change only constants. Arbitrary \(0<\varepsilon<1\) can be covered by a dyadic tolerance no larger than \(\varepsilon\). No compression requirement \(s<n\) is imposed in parameter regimes where the displayed allowance is already at least \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existential proposition above or its full logical negation. An affirmative proof must specify a single finite program and universal constants, formalize its seed-length and bit computations, establish the stated worst-case resource bounds, and prove the additive-error inequality for every permitted program and every parameter triple. A negative proof must rule out every such uniform program and choice of constants; a limitation of one construction, one analysis or one restricted generator class is insufficient. The theorem must use the stated ordinary uniform-seed distribution and arbitrary merging transitions. A result solely for weighted generators, hitting sets or a restricted branching-program subclass does not meet this target.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic algorithm A, a total computable function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), and an integer \(c\ge0\), such that A decides whether G contains a k-clique and uses at most \(f(k)(N+2)^c\) steps for every encoded pair (G,k) of total bit length N? The exponent c is independent of both k and G. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\) under parameterized many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A graph G is finite, simple and undirected, with vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), including n=0. A k-clique is a subset of exactly k vertices with an edge between each pair of distinct vertices. The empty subset is a 0-clique; no k-clique exists when k>n. For a fixed binary encoding, write \(1^n0\), then the n by n adjacency matrix in row order, then the ordinary binary representation of the nonnegative integer k (0 is written as 0, and otherwise there are no leading zeroes). A valid matrix is symmetric with zero diagonal, and the entire remaining suffix is the representation of k. N counts all bits, including k. A rejects any malformed string in time polynomial in its bit length. The bound in the statement applies to every valid pair, including k>n. The parameter is k alone; there is no promise on density, degree, clique number or any other graph property. A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input and initially blank work tapes; each transition reads or writes only at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The runtime includes parsing, input access and all internal work. Correctness is exact, and no advice, randomness, oracle or quantum operations are supplied. The same A, f and c work for every pair; f must be computable by a machine that halts on every nonnegative integer input, but its growth and the time needed to compute it have no prescribed bound. Constant multiplicative overhead can be absorbed into f. Using full input length rather than n gives the usual FPT question: for k at most n the two lengths are polynomially related, and k>n is rejected after parsing. For completeness, a parameterized language is a set of pairs \((x,k)\in\{0,1\}^*\times\mathbb N\), with both components explicitly encoded. It belongs to FPT if one uniform deterministic machine decides it within \(h(k)(M+2)^a\) steps for a total computable positive h, a fixed nonnegative integer a and complete encoding length M. A parameterized many-one reduction computes a single output pair \((y,k^{\prime})\) in such a time bound, preserves yes versus no membership, and satisfies \(k^{\prime}\le g(k)\) for a total computable function g; writing the output counts toward its runtime. The class W[1] can equivalently be defined as all parameterized languages admitting such a reduction to the Clique problem just specified. This characterization fixes the reduction convention without a change of target. It includes FPT, and Clique belongs to it, so FPT membership of Clique is equivalent to equality of the two classes.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of the single algorithm, computable multiplier and constant exponent in the statement, or prove their joint nonexistence. In the affirmative case, prove correctness and the uniform worst-case bound on all pairs, together with the malformed-input convention. In the negative case, exclude every such algorithm, computable f and exponent c; a conditional lower bound, a bound for a restricted algorithm model, or failure at one proposed multiplier and exponent does not settle this target. An algorithm whose polynomial exponent depends on k also does not satisfy the displayed quantifiers.

The checked fixed-k algorithm paper and its 2026 publication metadata provide no FPT algorithm. cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions: Fix an integer clause-width bound \(q\ge 3\). A q-CNF formula is a finite list of clauses, each a finite list of at most q literals. A literal is a variable \(x_i\) or its negation \(\neg x_i\), with \(1\le i\le n\). The variables that occur are exactly \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), so n counts distinct variables, not clauses or input bits. Repeated literals, repeated clauses and clauses containing both signs of a variable are allowed. A Boolean assignment satisfies the formula if every clause has at least one true literal. An empty clause is false; the empty conjunction is true and has n=0. For a completely specified binary encoding, let \(\operatorname{code}(a)\), for a nonnegative integer a, be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). Encode n and the number m of clauses with this code, then each clause by its coded length followed by its literals. Each literal is a sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negated) and the code of its variable index. All indicated lists must be fully present, with no trailing bits, valid indices and every declared variable occurring. Let L be the complete bit length. Ill-formed strings, including clauses wider than q, are rejected. No density, satisfiability-count, occurrence or input-distribution promise is imposed. A q-SAT decider A is one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program and fixed finite tape alphabets, a read-only input tape and initially blank work tapes. Each transition reads or writes only the cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. The total transition count includes parsing, input access and all internal work. A must halt on all inputs, decide satisfiability exactly on valid q-CNF formulas, and reject malformed strings in polynomial time in their length. It receives no advice, random bits, quantum operations, oracle or precomputed instance information. The machine may depend on the fixed q. For a valid formula F, let \(t_A(F)\) be its runtime and \(n(F),L(F)\) its variable count and bit length. An exponent \(\alpha\ge 0\) is attainable at width q if there exist such a decider A and fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\) with \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{\alpha n(F)}(L(F)+1)^d\) for every valid q-CNF formula F. The constants are independent of F. Define \(s_q\) as the infimum of all attainable exponents. This set is nonempty because exhaustive assignment testing gives an attainable exponent 1, so \(0\le s_q\le1\). The infimum need not itself be attainable. Polynomial factors in L remain explicit, including when clauses are repeated many times. The chosen explicit syntax and malformed-input normalization do not impose a new satisfiability promise; they fix the bit model for the source’s exponential-rate question. This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(L(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on epsilon. This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from epsilon to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. cards.title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every integer \(1\le k\le |V|, A(G,k)\) outputs a set \(S\subseteq V\) with |\(S|=k\) and |\(E(G[S])|\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)/C\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max _{T\subseteq V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|\)?
cards.definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. \(G[S]\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with \(n=|V|\) or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree \(2|E(G[S])|/k\), or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants \(\varepsilon ,\delta >0\) with \(\varepsilon +\delta <1\), does there exist an integer \(q\ge 2\) such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and \(\operatorname{val}(G)\) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). An edge \(e=(u,v)\) carries an explicitly given permutation \(\pi _{e}:[q]\to [q]\) and is satisfied exactly when \(\pi _{e}(\ell (u))=\ell (v)\). Thus \(\operatorname{val}(G)=\max _{\ell} |\){e satisfied by \(\ell\)}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the \(\ge 1- \varepsilon\) case and every unsatisfiable formula into the \(\le \delta\) case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on \(\varepsilon ,\delta\). Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Deterministic competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), determine the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. Give a real-valued function \(g\) and a complete Lean proof that
\[\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1},\qquad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le\frac1{100}.\]
The tolerance is absolute in the competitive ratio and is the same for every \(k\).
cards.definitions:
A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify an unambiguous function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of
\[\forall k\ge1,\quad |g(k)-R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)|\le1/100.\]
Both sides of the error interval must be proved with the metric, rule, additive-constant and sequence quantifiers above. In particular, certified functions \(\ell,u\) satisfying \(\ell(k)\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u(k)\) and \(u(k)-\ell(k)\le1/50\) for every positive integer \(k\) qualify through their midpoint. Exact determination also qualifies. An upper bound on an infimum must not silently be replaced by existence of a rule attaining its endpoint.

The absolute error must remain at most \(1/100\) as \(k\) grows; relative error \(k/100\), a constant-factor asymptotic estimate, or finitely many solved server counts does not meet it. A rule for a particular metric family or one named algorithm establishes only the corresponding restricted guarantee. A lower bound must rule out all allowed deterministic rules on its witnessing metric, rather than only one proposed algorithm or proof certificate. No unproved additional hypothesis is part of the target. There is no fixed formula grammar or polynomial evaluation requirement for \(g\), but repeating the defining infimum without determining its value is not an answer. The benchmark precision does not assert the classical exact equality \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) or endpoint attainment.

cards.title: Optimal approximation ratio for unrelated-machine makespan
cards.formal:
For offline makespan minimization on unrelated parallel machines, determine the real number
\[\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}=\inf\mathcal R,\qquad \mathcal R=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\exists A\ \exists c,k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall I\in\mathcal I,\ \begin{array}{l} A(I)\text{ halts in at most }c(L(I)+2)^k\text{ bit steps,}\\ A(I)\text{ outputs a feasible schedule }\sigma_I,\\ C_{\max}(\sigma_I)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\end{array}\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal I\) is the full class of finite rational processing-time matrices defined below, \(L(I)\) is the full binary input length, and \(A\) ranges over finite deterministic Turing-machine programs. Approximate \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\) within absolute error \(1/100\), with a complete Lean proof. No complexity hypothesis is included in the definition of this number.
cards.definitions:
An instance has integers \(m\ge1\), \(n\ge0\), machine set \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), job set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and a fully listed matrix \(p\in(\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\})^{m\times n}\). Set \([0]=\varnothing\). Each job has at least one finite entry. The symbol \(\infty\) forbids that machine–job assignment; it is not an arithmetic input with finite cost. Entries may differ arbitrarily between both machines and jobs. All processing times use the same time unit.

A feasible schedule is a function \(\sigma:[n]\to[m]\) such that \(p_{\sigma(j),j}<\infty\) for every job. Its load on machine \(i\) is \(\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij}\), with an empty sum equal to zero. Define
\[C_{\max}(\sigma)=\max_{i\in[m]}\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i}p_{ij},\qquad \operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{\sigma\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(\sigma).\]
This minimum is finite and attained because the feasible set is finite and nonempty. Jobs are independent, available at time zero and indivisible. A machine executes its assigned jobs consecutively, one at a time, without preemption; their order does not affect the objective. There are no release dates, precedence constraints, setup times, communication costs or additional scheduling promises. For \(n=0\), the unique empty assignment has makespan zero.

Fix the following concrete binary encoding. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(E(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\), where juxtaposition denotes concatenation. A finite entry \(a/b\) is represented in lowest terms with \(a\ge0\), \(b\ge1\), as the tag bit \(0\) followed by \(E(a)E(b)\); \(\infty\) is the single tag bit \(1\). The input is \(E(m)E(n)\) followed by the \(mn\) entry encodings in row order. Its total bit length is \(L(I)\). The output is \(E(\sigma(1))\cdots E(\sigma(n))\) in job order; the empty schedule has an empty output. Equivalent ordinary encodings with polynomial-time translations give the same approximation-ratio infimum.

A program is a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice, random bits, optimization oracle or noncomputable constants. Input reading, work-tape computation and writing the full output count toward its bit running time. Arithmetic on the encoded rationals must be performed within that bound; an arbitrary-precision arithmetic operation is not a unit-cost primitive. Guarantees are required on every valid instance; invalid strings are outside \(\mathcal I\). The algorithm receives the complete matrix in advance, regardless of the category’s historical online-algorithms label.

For each fixed achieved ratio \(r\), the same program and constants \(c,k\) must work for all \(m,n,p\). They may depend on \(r\), but \(r\) is not additional advice or an input to the program. A different program for each input length is not allowed. The set \(\mathcal R\) concerns an absolute multiplicative guarantee on each instance, with no additive slack and no asymptotic or average-case exception. If \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)=0\), the output must also have makespan zero; no quotient by zero is used. All these conventions include empty instances.

The ratio is dimensionless. The established factor-two algorithm gives \(2\in\mathcal R\), so \(\mathcal R\) is nonempty and \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le2\). The infimum need not be attained: \(\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\), for \(u\ge1\), means that for every \(\eta>0\) some program achieves a ratio at most \(u+\eta\), without requiring one program to attain \(u\) or one uniform procedure generating all these programs. A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that no program achieves any fixed \(r\in[1,\ell)\) on every instance. The numerical tolerance applies to this infimum, not to the feasibility or objective guarantee of a proposed schedule.
cards.answer_criterion:
Specify a real value \(a\) and give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[|a-\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}|\le\frac1{100}.\]
Both sides of the claimed error interval must be certified for the full deterministic polynomial-bit-time model above. In particular, proved bounds \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{unrel}}\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\) qualify through \(a=(\ell+u)/2\); exact determination also qualifies. Upper and lower bounds must have the infimum quantifiers specified above, without silently requiring attainment or substituting a fixed machine count. An unambiguous mathematical expression or certified specification of \(a\) is acceptable without a decimal expansion, but simply restating the defining optimization is not a determination. A one-sided algorithmic improvement or relaxation gap alone does not meet the criterion.

No unproved complexity assumption is implicit in this target. A theorem proved only under \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) is a conditional bound, not an unconditional certification of this number. An answer expressed by cases must establish the required error bound in every case. Here \(\mathrm P\) denotes languages decided by deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines and \(\mathrm{NP}\) languages having polynomial-length witnesses verified in polynomial time. The \(1/100\) allowance is benchmark precision on the ratio; it need not decide whether the exact infimum equals two.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed real \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), with \(k_n=\lfloor n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\rfloor\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) for which \[\Pr[\widehat b=b]\geq\frac23\] in the balanced one-graph experiment below for every sufficiently large integer \(n\).
cards.definitions:
For \(n\geq2\), let \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_n\) is the distribution of a simple undirected labeled graph on \([n]\) in which each unordered pair of distinct vertices is an edge independently with probability \(1/2\). For \(0\leq k\leq n\), the planted distribution \(P_{n,k}\) chooses \(S\) uniformly among all \(k\)-element subsets of \([n]\), includes every edge inside \(S\), and chooses each other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). There are no loops. The planted set has exactly \(k\) vertices; it is not formed by independently including each vertex.

In the experiment, first choose a fair bit \(b\). If \(b=0\), sample \(G\sim N_n\); if \(b=1\), sample \(G\sim P_{n,k_n}\). Give \(A\) only \((n,k_n,G)\), and let \(\widehat b\in\{0,1\}\) be its output. All randomness of the sampling and of \(A\) is independent. Success is averaged over \(b\), the graph, the planted set when present and the algorithm’s random bits. Writing \(s_A(n,\varepsilon)\) for this probability, \[s_A(n,\varepsilon)=\tfrac12\big(\Pr_{G\sim N_n,A}[A(n,k_n,G)=0]+\Pr_{G\sim P_{n,k_n},A}[A(n,k_n,G)=1]\big).\] This is not a separate \(2/3\) guarantee on each individual graph or on each of the two distributions. The algorithm receives one sampled graph, without the label \(b\), the set \(S\), sample access to the unknown distribution or other side information.

For \(u\geq0\), define \(\operatorname{code}(u)=1^a0\operatorname{bin}(u+1)\), where the binary expansion has \(a\) bits and no leading zeroes. The input is \(1^n0\operatorname{code}(k)\), followed by the full \(n^2\) adjacency matrix in row order, with no trailing bits. A valid input has \(n\geq2\), \(0\leq k\leq n\), a symmetric matrix and zero diagonal; let \(L\) be its full bit length. An allowed algorithm is one probabilistic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program and tape alphabet, using fresh independent fair bits and no oracle or advice. For some integers \(C,c\geq1\), on every input and every random-bit sequence it outputs one bit within \(C(L+1)^c\) transitions. Malformed encodings return 0 within this bound. Input processing, bit arithmetic and any additional graphs generated by the algorithm count toward time. On valid inputs \(L=\Theta(n^2)\), so polynomial time in \(L\) and in \(n\) are equivalent.

For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), the forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N\ \forall n\geq N:\ s_A(n,\varepsilon)\geq2/3\), with the global clock condition just specified. The program and constants may depend on this fixed \(\varepsilon\), but cannot change with \(n\); \(\varepsilon\) is not supplied as an oracle or an infinite advice string. The supplied integer \(k_n\) removes any need to compute a real power to construct the input. The conjecture therefore says that every allowed algorithm has success below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). It does not assert that its success tends to \(1/2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-verified proof of this hardness proposition or its logical negation. To refute it, give some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), one allowed polynomial-time algorithm and a proof that its balanced success is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large \(n\). To prove it, exclude every such algorithm for every fixed \(\varepsilon\). Success only on infinitely many sizes does not satisfy the refutation target. A limitation on sum-of-squares relaxations, local searches or another restricted model does not establish hardness against all allowed machines. A recovery result must imply the stated detection guarantee; a change of planting distribution or a conditional theorem must not be treated as an unconditional resolution of this exact experiment.
cards.status_note: No unconditional proof or unrestricted polynomial-time refutation of this exact fixed-size, balanced constant-success hypothesis was located in a bounded check through 14 September 2026. The cited sum-of-squares theorem is a relaxation/refutation lower bound; the optimal-advantage and September 2026 topology results are conditional, and several newer recovery results use other random graph models. Source/model review does not independently certify every cited proof.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.formal:
Is the following implication true in the ordinary uniform Turing-machine model?
\[\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\exists L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \exists S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\ :\ (L,D^S)\notin\mathrm{AvgP}.
\]
Here \(S\) is one exact polynomial-time sampler, \(D^S=(D^S_n)_{n\ge1}\) its output distribution ensemble, and \(\mathrm{AvgP}\) means deterministic, always-correct computation with the positive-moment runtime bound below. Thus the conclusion requires one fixed language and one fixed feasible sampling procedure for which no exact deterministic decider has average polynomial running time. No additional hardness or derandomization hypothesis may be assumed.
cards.definitions:
All algorithms have one fixed finite program, use ordinary multitape Turing machines with finite tape alphabets and unit-cost transitions, and receive explicit binary strings. There is no oracle or nonuniform advice. Randomized machines obtain independent fair coin bits; reading input, generating coins, computing intermediate data and writing output all take time.

A language is a set \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\). It belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if one deterministic machine decides membership on every input \(x\) within \(a(|x|+1)^d\) steps for fixed positive integers \(a,d\). It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(a,d\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary certificate \(y\) of length at most \(a(|x|+1)^d\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). The verifier is total and polynomial time in its full input length. The premise concerns these total decision classes.

A sampler \(S\in\mathrm{PSamp}\) is one randomized machine which, on unary input \(1^n\), \(n\ge1\), halts on every random tape within \(q(n)=a(n+1)^d\) steps, for fixed positive integers \(a,d\) depending on \(S\). It outputs a finite binary string of length at most \(q(n)\), possibly the empty string. Put \(D^S_n(x)=\Pr[S(1^n)=x]\). Sampling is exact, not an approximation, and its time bound holds for every coin sequence. The parameter \(n\) need not equal the sampled string length. These probabilities form a finite distribution: one may regard the random tape as \(q(n)\) fair bits, with unused bits ignored.

An exact decider \(A\) for \(L\) is one deterministic machine that, on the explicitly separated pair \((1^n,x)\), halts and returns \(1\) exactly when \(x\in L\), for every \(n\ge1\) and every binary string \(x\), including strings of zero probability under \(D^S_n\). It cannot answer 'unknown'. Let \(T_A(1^n,x)\) be its number of transitions, charged at least one step. There is no worst-case polynomial-time requirement on this decider. By definition,
\[(L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists A\ \exists\eta>0\ \exists C>0\ \exists k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge1:
\sum_x D^S_n(x)T_A(1^n,x)^{\eta}\le C(n+1)^k,
\]
where \(A\) must be an exact decider and \(\eta,C\) are real constants. The sum is over the finite support of \(D^S_n\). The algorithm and constants may depend on \(L,S\) but not on \(n\). Nonmembership means that for every such \(A,\eta,C,k\), some \(n\ge1\) violates the inequality. It is not necessary to violate it at every sufficiently large length.

This is the positive-moment convention for average polynomial time. It allows \(\eta\ne1\); the definition is not a bound on expected runtime itself and does not permit incorrect membership answers. The existentially selected sampler is part of the distributional problem, not input to the decider, which may have its fixed description built into its program.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication or its logical negation, under the stated uniform models and quantifiers. An affirmative result must, from \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) alone, establish a fixed \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) and a fixed exact strict-polynomial-time sampler for which every deterministic exact decider fails every positive-moment polynomial bound. The sampler and language cannot depend on the decider being challenged. A negative result must prove \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) together with \((L,D^S)\in\mathrm{AvgP}\) for every permitted \(L,S\); an oracle separation or a barrier for one reduction method is not that negation. A complete proof of the implication may use the premise without separately proving it. Partial improvements, an additional unproved hardness assumption, or a failure of one particular algorithm do not establish the target.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and every integer \(q\ge \Delta +2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(n\ge 1\) and \(\Omega\)={\(\sigma :V(G)\to [q] : \sigma (u)\ne \sigma (v)\) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from \(V(G)\), then choose a colour uniformly from \([q]\)\\(\{\sigma (u):u\in N(v)\}\) and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega\). Define \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min \{t\in Z_{\ge 0}: \max _{\sigma \in \Omega} (1/2)\sum_{\tau \in \Omega}|\mathrm{P}^{t}(\sigma ,\tau )- \pi (\tau )|\le 1/4\}\). This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of \(n, \Delta , q\) and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

cards.title: Kannan–Tetali–Vempala conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(K,c>0\) exist such that, for all \(r,s\ge 1\) and all nonnegative integer margins \(a\in \mathbb{N} ^{r},b\in \mathbb{N} ^{s}\) with a nonempty realization set \(\Omega (a,b)\), the lazy switch chain below satisfies \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le K(r+s)^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.
